title: Out of nothing
hookLine: creation out of nothing: the world isn't God and isn't an accident, but a gift

cards: A potter needs clay. A carpenter needs wood. A cook needs at least an egg.
The makers we meet start with something already there, and shape it. So Christians have asked a strange question: when God made the world, what was the clay?

The first line of the Bible doesn't stop to say: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." No workshop, no pile of material, no rival standing by. Christian teaching came to answer with three words.

teach.b: Out of nothing. In Latin, ex nihilo.
The teaching is that God didn't shape the world from something already lying around. Before creation there was God, and nothing else.
The letter to the Hebrews puts it this way: "the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear."
Paul, in Romans, describes God as one who "calleth those things which be not as though they were." A voice, and then a world. Christian teachers draw two lines from this.
First: the world is not God. It isn't a piece of God broken off, or God's body. A tree is a tree, a river is a river; they're made, and God is the maker.

teach.h: THE WORLD IS NOT AN ACCIDENT.
teach.b: Second: the world is not an accident. Nothing forced God's hand. There was no raw stuff that had to be used up, no rival who had to be beaten.
So why make anything at all? In Revelation the elders before the throne sing: "thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created."
Some Christian writers read that pleasure as love: a world made because love likes to share.
Between those two lines sits a third word: gift. If the world isn't God, it can be studied, used, cared for. If it isn't an accident, it was meant.
Something meant, and handed over, is a gift. That turns an ordinary object into a quiet question: not just what is this for, but who gave this?

how: Christians confess God as maker in the creeds, which begin with God the Father, maker of heaven and earth, and some give thanks before meals or at the start of the day for what they receive.

practice: Hold whatever is closest, a mug, a pen, an apple, your own hand, and look at it as if you'd never seen it.

Trace it backward, who made it, what it's made of, where that came from, until the chain runs out of answers, and stay there a moment. If you pray, give thanks for it by name; if not, just say quietly: this was given.

wordCard.voice: Out of nothing. The teaching that God made the world from no material at all: not God, not an accident, but a gift.

orig.note: Hebrew: created. The verb in the Bible's first line: God created the heaven and the earth.

carryVoice: Your line: from nothing, for love. Every made thing can be a quiet question. See you tomorrow.
